title: Mesa County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Mesa County wells have a median depth of 79 ft and reported yield of 8 gpm. See local drilling costs, water-level records and checks before buying.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Mesa County
intro_html:
A shallow well near your property does not guarantee a shallow drilling bill. Mesa County’s recorded well depths have a median of 79 ft, but the middle half spans 23-262 ft. That is a wide spread for anyone budgeting a rural home or land purchase.

Colorado DWR records contain 6,388 permitted wells in the county, with 3,149 recorded as constructed. These are not all household water supplies: monitoring accounts for 39% of the use mix. Start with the county figures, then narrow your research to comparable wells around Grand Junction, Glade Park, Collbran or wherever the parcel actually sits.

sections.heading: A 79-Foot Median Hides Mesa County’s Depth Range
sections.html:
Of the 3,670 wells reporting depth, 55% are under 100 ft. Still, the middle half runs from 23-262 ft, and the 90th-percentile depth is 490 ft. A bid based only on the county median leaves substantial room for added drilling. Ask how the price changes if usable water requires going deeper.

The ground is mixed sedimentary and alluvial material. Most permits fall under the unnamed / fractured-bedrock aquifer category, while 119 name Alluvial and 17 name Entrada. Those broad labels do not establish conditions beneath a particular lot. Fracture connections and water-bearing layers can change locally, so compare construction logs near Fruita, Mesa or De Beque rather than treating the entire county as the same drilling ground.

sections.heading: Reported Yield Is Useful, but Test the Household Supply
sections.html:
The 1,089 records with pump yields show a median of 8.0 gpm and a middle half of 5.0-15.0 gpm. That gives a buyer a useful starting point, not a guarantee of sustained household supply. A reported pumping rate needs context: how the well was tested, how far the water drew down and how it recovered.

At the low end, 3% report less than 1 gpm, and 20% fall in the 1-5 gpm category. Low production deserves attention before closing, because storage and demand management may become part of the system. Have the well tested against your intended use, and confirm that the permit authorizes that use. Physical production does not establish permission to irrigate or water livestock.

sections.heading: Mesa County Water Levels Do Not Show a Simple Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to standing water before pumping, not the drilled depth. Among 419 reporting records, the median is 40 ft below ground and the middle half is 15-162 ft. A shallow standing level does not mean the well is shallow or that it will maintain that level under demand.

Decade medians move from 25 ft in the 1970s to 100 ft in the 1990s, 17 ft in the 2000s, 30 ft in the 2010s and 73 ft in the 2020s. Recent medians are deeper, but the full series fluctuates. This is not evidence of a steady countywide water-table decline. Measurements from different wells and locations cannot substitute for repeated measurements at the property you are buying.

sections.heading: Permit History and Driller Names in Mesa County
sections.html:
Mesa County’s permit history includes 1,295 permits issued in the 1990s and 1,530 in the 2000s, followed by 1,134 in the 2010s. The records include 726 from the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, so its smaller total should not be read as a direct measure of declining demand.

Prominent driller entries include Rocky Mtn Drilling And Pump Services Llc (Logue, James M.) with 329 records and Rocky Mountain Drlg./Pump Svcs (Wisener, A. L.) with 283. These are historical record labels, not confirmation of current availability. With domestic/household use accounting for 45% and monitoring for 39%, select nearby household construction logs when evaluating a contractor’s experience with your likely well conditions.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well on Mesa County Ground
sections.html:
The drilling model for Mesa County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground uses $50-$75 per foot. At the 79 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $4,000-$5,900. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $10,000-$17,900.

Those figures are a planning allowance, not a parcel-specific quote. The 23-262 ft middle-half depth range is the reason to get a written per-foot rate and clear terms for additional depth. Ask what the bid includes for casing, grout, access, pump installation and trenching. On a Glade Park or Collbran lot, walk the proposed rig route and utility route with the contractor before assuming the median-depth finished price covers your site.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality, Low Yield and the Septic Layout
sections.html:
The mapped environmental inventory within about 10 miles includes 82 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 23 historic mine features and 38 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. These counts flag questions to investigate; they do not establish contamination in a particular well. Review each relevant site’s location and findings, then choose water testing with help from the local health department or a qualified laboratory.

Check the well’s casing, sanitary seal and grout as well as its production. A permit or a neighboring successful well does not guarantee a productive bore on vacant land. Before setting the house footprint, have the proposed well and septic locations reviewed for required separation and practical construction access. An existing system should be inspected rather than assumed sound because water comes out of the tap.

sections.heading: Before Buying in Orchard Mesa, Loma or the Redlands
sections.html:
Match the parcel to its actual DWR permit, construction log and available pump records. Countywide statistics are background; comparable nearby wells are the better starting point for a drilling conversation. Around Orchard Mesa, Loma or the Redlands, look for records with similar ground conditions and intended use, not simply the closest map marker.

For an existing home, request a current production assessment and water-quality testing before committing. For vacant land, confirm the permitting path before designing around a private well. An exempt household-use permit does not automatically authorize outdoor watering, and some proposed uses may require augmentation. Make the purchase decision with a workable well location, septic layout, access plan and written drilling scope—not just an assurance that neighbors have water.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Mesa County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 79 ft, and the middle half of reported depths runs from 23-262 ft. The 90th-percentile depth is 490 ft. That spread makes nearby construction logs more useful than the county median for pricing a particular parcel. Compare wells in similar ground and with similar intended uses.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Mesa County?
faq.a: The county cost model uses $50-$75 per foot. At the median depth of 79 ft, the drilled hole is about $4,000-$5,900, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $10,000-$17,900. Actual bids depend on depth, ground conditions, access and the installation scope.

faq.q: How much water does a well produce in Mesa County?
faq.a: Reported pump yield has a median of 8.0 gpm, with the middle half at 5.0-15.0 gpm. These figures come from 1,089 reporting records, not every permitted well. Because 3% report less than 1 gpm, a buyer should verify sustained production, drawdown and recovery rather than rely on an old reported pumping rate.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Mesa County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established at the individual well through testing and inspection. The mapped inventory within about 10 miles includes 82 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 38 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, but proximity alone does not prove contamination. Review relevant site findings, inspect the well’s sanitary condition and arrange appropriate laboratory testing before relying on the water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Mesa County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady countywide decline. Median depth to water was 100 ft in the 1990s, 17 ft in the 2000s, 30 ft in the 2010s and 73 ft in the 2020s. These groups contain different measurements, so repeated readings from the same well are needed to assess a local trend.
